Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 162 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2022) 
Background 
Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 162 (Berry WMU), is found in east central AB and is part of the Southern management 
region. This unit is relatively large, and covers an area of 4,761.5 km2. The WMU includes land south of Highway 9, east of 
Highway 36, and west of the Alberta/Saskatchewan border. The southern boundary follows a series of roads including 
Township Road 25-0, Secondary Road 886, Township Road 25-4, Highway 41, and Highway 570. Several creeks and 
drainages pass through the WMU, with the major waterbodies consisting primarily of irrigation reservoirs, or shallow lakes fed 
by runoff. The WMU is within the dry mixedgrass subregion, and contains large expanses of cultivated cropland and native 
grassland. Much of the WMU is deeded land, however large parcels of crown owned native grassland under grazing lease are 
also present. Oil and gas development remains established throughout the WMU, and in recent years, renewable energy 
development has increased. The WMU also contains an open pit coal mine operation near Highway 36. Chronic Wasting 
Disease (CWD) is well established within the WMU, with an overall prevalence between 31% and 55% from samples 
submitted in 2019. The established population goal for WMU 162 is a pre-hunting season population of 2,400 mule deer and 
800 white-tailed deer. 
A survey for ungulates (mule deer, white-tailed deer, and moose) was last conducted for WMU 162 in 2014 using a similar 
transect methodology, so results can be directly compared (Table 1). 
The objective of the January 2022 survey was to assess the status of the ungulate population in WMU 162 by determining 
estimates for abundance, density and age-sex composition. We also recorded observations of additional species of game 
management or conservation concern including elk, pronghorn, carnivores, game birds, and sensitive or at risk species. 
Survey method 
A rotary wing transect survey was conducted January 10-14, 2022, flying 74 north-south lines at 1.6 km intervals, which 
obtained 50% coverage (800 m wide survey strip), for a total survey effort of 2,786 km. At each observation point, ungulates 
were classified by species, and when possible, determined sex and age was recorded. Antler size for deer was classified as 
‘small’ (spike or two points on one or both antlers), ‘medium’ (antlers with 3 or more points; antlers inside ears) or large 
(antlers with ≥ 4 points, antlers outside of ears). Because transects varied in length, the average density (R; #/km2) of mule 
deer, white-tailed deer, and moose was calculated by summing the total animals counted per transect (Σx) by total area 
searched (length of transects multiplied by 800 m survey strip [Σz]) (see Krebs 2014, Jolly 1969). For a population estimate 
(unequal sized units, sampling without replacement), the average density (R) was multiplied by the overall area of the WMU 
(Z). The width of the 90% confidence interval was calculated by multiplying the t statistic for the left-tailed inverse of the 
Student’s t-distribution, (t0.05,df=n-1) by standard error (SE; without replacement) of the abundance estimate where SE=sq 
root variance, and variance=N*(N-n)/(n*(n-1))*(Σx2+R2*Σz2-2*R*Σxz) with N as the total number of possible transects given 
100% coverage, and n as the number of transects sampled. 
Results 
Mule deer 
A total of 1,183 mule deer were observed in 158 groups (range 1-28). The estimated density was 0.53 mule deer/km2 and the 
estimated abundance was 2,528 individuals (90% CI 2,124 – 2,932), representing a 7% decrease from the population estimate 
in 2014. A total of 1,167 mule deer were successfully classified and the buck:doe:fawn ratio was estimated to be 58:100:65. 
That results in an estimated 2021/2022 early winter mule deer population of 661 bucks, 1,131 does, and 736 fawns. Of the 
308 mule deer bucks classified, 138 (45%) were classified ‘small’, 102 (34%) ‘medium’, and 65 (21%) ‘large’. This result 
indicates the WMU 162 mule deer population is close to the established management goal, and results are similar to the 
survey conducted in 2014.

White-tailed deer 
A total of 445 white-tailed deer were observed in 56 groups (range 1-36). The estimated density was 0.20 deer/km2 and the 
estimated abundance was 951 individuals (90% CI 627 – 1,275), representing a 47% decrease from the population estimate in 
2014. A total of 380 white-tailed deer were successfully classified and the buck:doe:fawn ratio was estimated to be 33:100:78. 
That results in an estimated 2021/2022 early winter white-tailed deer population of 150 bucks, 451 does, and 350 fawns. Of 
the 60 white-tailed deer bucks classified, 25 (42%) were classified ‘small’, 25 (42%) ‘medium’, and 10 (16%) ‘large’. This result 
indicates the WMU 162 white-tailed deer population is close to the established management goal, however populations have 
decreased substantially since the survey conducted in 2014. 
Moose 
A total of 25 moose were observed in 8 groups (range 1-5). The estimated density was 0.01 moose/km2 and the estimated 
abundance was 53 individuals (90% CI 29 – 78). All 25 moose were successfully classified and the bull:cow:calf ratio was 
estimated to be 100:100:113. That results in an estimated 2021/2022 early winter moose population of 17 bulls, 17 cows, and 
19 calves. When interpreting the data, consideration should be given to the low sample of moose observed and how it may 
impact population, density, and sex ratio estimates. The survey results demonstrates there is a relatively low abundance of 
moose in the WMU, however numbers are similar to the survey conducted in 2014. 
Other species observations that occurred within the survey area include 336 sharp-tailed grouse, 205 pronghorn, 118 coyote, 
58 Hungarian partridge, 13 porcupine, two red fox, two golden eagle, one short-eared owl, one snowy owl, and 423 Canada 
geese. Two coyote dens were also observed
